It is less convincing than the motion dazzle idea.
It sounds too strange and has very little evidence behind it.
It is the best supported but may not be the only answer.
questions.explanation: She calls it the front-runner while noting that stripes could serve more than one purpose.

intro: Listen to a talk in an entomology class.
talk: Today's topic is one of the strangest life cycles in the animal world. In eastern North America, there are periodical cicadas that spend either thirteen or seventeen years underground as nymphs, feeding on sap from tree roots. Then, in a single spring, millions of them emerge at once, sometimes more than a million per acre. They mate, lay eggs, and die within a few weeks. So, two questions. Why emerge all together, and why such long cycles? The first question has a fairly accepted answer: predator satiation. Birds, squirrels, and other predators feast on the cicadas, but there are so many that the predators simply get full, and most cicadas survive. Now, the second question is more debated. Notice that thirteen and seventeen are both prime numbers. One explanation is that prime cycles help avoid predators with shorter cycles of their own. If a predator's population peaks every two or three years, a seventeen-year cicada will rarely emerge in one of those peak years. Another explanation focuses on hybridization. If a thirteen-year brood and a seventeen-year brood share a region, they emerge together only once every two hundred twenty-one years. Mixing broods could produce offspring with mismatched timing, so prime cycles would keep broods separate. Here's the catch. Neither hypothesis has been directly tested, partly because, well, a single experiment would take up a researcher's entire career.

questions.prompt: What is the talk mainly about?
options: How cicada nymphs feed on tree roots underground
Why cicadas are an important food source for birds and squirrels
Explanations for the unusual life cycle of periodical cicadas
How scientists count insects in a single area
questions.explanation: The professor discusses why the cicadas emerge together and why their cycles are prime numbers.

questions.prompt: According to the professor, why do the cicadas emerge all at once?
options: Their eggs hatch only when the soil becomes warm.
So many emerge that predators cannot eat them all.
Predators avoid areas crowded with large insects.
Their emergence matches the cycles of predators.
questions.explanation: Predator satiation means predators get full and most cicadas survive.

questions.prompt: What does the hybridization explanation propose?
options: Prime cycles let different broods mix and produce stronger offspring.
Prime cycles help cicadas avoid predators with short cycles.
Prime cycles match the timing of seasonal changes in trees.
Prime cycles keep different broods from emerging together often.
questions.explanation: Thirteen- and seventeen-year broods coincide only every two hundred twenty-one years, limiting mixing.

questions.prompt: Why does the professor mention a researcher's entire career?
options: To explain why the hypotheses are difficult to test
To show how long it took to discover prime cycles
To suggest that cicada research is losing support
To emphasize how long a single cicada can live
questions.explanation: With cycles of thirteen or seventeen years, one experiment would take decades, so the ideas remain untested.

intro: Listen to a talk in an ornithology class.
talk: Okay, so most birds put enormous effort into raising their young. But some species have found a way to skip all that work. It's called brood parasitism, when a bird lays its eggs in another species' nest and leaves the host to raise its chicks. The best-known example is the common cuckoo in Europe. Here's how it goes. A female cuckoo watches a host nest, say, of a reed warbler. When the host is away, she swoops in, removes one of the host's eggs, and lays one of her own, all in a matter of seconds. And her egg often closely matches the color and pattern of the host's eggs. Now, the cuckoo chick usually hatches first, and within hours, it does something rather brutal. It pushes the host's eggs, one by one, out of the nest. So the host parents end up raising a single cuckoo chick, which can grow much bigger than they are. Why don't the hosts notice? Well, many do. Some hosts learn to recognize and reject foreign eggs. And that sets off what biologists call an evolutionary arms race. Hosts get better at spotting fake eggs, so cuckoos evolve better mimicry, which pushes hosts to become even more discriminating. Interestingly, though, hosts rarely reject the chick itself, even when it looks nothing like their own.

options: How reed warblers build and protect their nests from predators
How some birds get other species to raise their young
Why cuckoo chicks grow larger than other birds
How birds learn to recognize their own eggs
questions.explanation: The professor describes brood parasitism by cuckoos and the hosts' responses.

questions.prompt: What does the female cuckoo do when she visits a host nest?
options: She removes every host egg and lays several of her own.
She waits until the host eggs hatch before laying.
She replaces the host's chicks with her own eggs.
She removes a host egg and lays one of her own.
questions.explanation: The professor says she removes one host egg and lays her own in a matter of seconds.

It imitates the calls of the host chicks.
It leaves the nest to find its real parents.

questions.explanation: Within hours of hatching, the chick pushes the host's eggs out one by one.

They usually abandon nests that hold a cuckoo chick.
They are better at detecting foreign eggs than foreign chicks.
They have stopped evolving defenses against cuckoos.
questions.explanation: Many hosts learn to reject foreign eggs, yet they rarely reject the cuckoo chick itself.

intro: Listen to a talk in an oceanography class.
talk: So, if you look at a map of the world's most productive fisheries, you'll notice something odd. Several of the richest ones lie off the western coasts of continents, places like Peru, California, and southwestern Africa. Why there? The answer is a process called upwelling, the rising of cold, deep water to the surface. Now, why does deep water matter? In the open ocean, the sunlit surface layer tends to run out of nutrients, like nitrate and phosphate, because plankton use them up and their remains sink. Meanwhile, those nutrients pile up in the dark water below, where there's no light for plants to use them. So you've got light on top and nutrients below. Upwelling brings the two together. Here's how it works off Peru, for instance. Winds blow along the coast toward the equator. But because of Earth's rotation, the surface water doesn't move straight with the wind. It's deflected, and on these coasts, it's pushed away from shore. And as surface water moves offshore, cold, nutrient-rich water rises from below to replace it. It's a bit like sliding the top sheet off a stack of papers: whatever's underneath is exposed. With nutrients and sunlight together, phytoplankton bloom, and that feeds everything from small fish to seabirds. But when those winds weaken, as they do during El Niño events off Peru, upwelling slows and fisheries can collapse.

questions.prompt: What is the talk mainly about?
options: How fishing has reduced plankton along coasts
How rising deep water supports rich fisheries
Why the open ocean contains so many nutrients
How El Niño changes the direction of winds
questions.explanation: The professor explains how coastal upwelling brings nutrients into sunlit water and supports fisheries.

questions.prompt: According to the professor, why does the ocean's surface layer often lack nutrients?
options: Sunlight breaks the nutrients down quickly.
Winds carry the nutrients away from shore.
Plankton use them up and their remains sink.
Cold water keeps nutrients from dissolving.
questions.explanation: The professor says plankton use up surface nutrients and their remains sink to deeper water.

questions.prompt: What causes surface water to move away from the coast of Peru?
options: Cold water sinking close to the shore
Large rivers carrying fresh water into the ocean from land
Warm currents arriving from the equator
Winds along the coast combined with Earth's rotation
questions.explanation: Winds blowing toward the equator, deflected by Earth's rotation, push surface water offshore.

questions.prompt: Why does the professor mention sliding the top sheet off a stack of papers?
options: To illustrate how removing surface water exposes deeper water
To show how plankton remains slowly sink down to the dark ocean floor
To explain why the winds blow along the coast
To compare ocean layers with rock layers on land
questions.explanation: Like removing the top sheet, moving surface water offshore exposes the water beneath.

intro: Listen to a talk in a meteorology class.
talk: Let's start by clearing up a popular myth. You may have heard that water drains from a sink clockwise in one hemisphere and counterclockwise in the other. It doesn't, at least not reliably. The direction depends on the shape of the sink and how the water was moving to begin with. But the effect behind that myth is real; it just works on a much larger scale. It's called the Coriolis effect. Because Earth rotates, anything moving freely over long distances appears to curve: to the right in the Northern Hemisphere, and to the left in the Southern. Picture throwing a ball across a spinning merry-go-round. To someone riding it, the ball seems to swerve, though it's really moving straight. Now, apply this to a hurricane. At the center is very low pressure, so air rushes inward from all sides. But in the Northern Hemisphere, each stream of air is deflected to the right, so instead of flowing straight in, the air swirls around the center counterclockwise. In the Southern Hemisphere, the spin is clockwise. The Coriolis effect is zero right at the equator and weak close to it. So hurricanes almost never form within about five degrees of the equator, despite warm water. As for your sink, over such short times and distances, the effect is far too weak to matter.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of the talk?
options: To show that sinks drain in opposite directions in each hemisphere
To explain how Earth's rotation affects large-scale air movement
To describe how hurricanes gain energy from warm ocean water
To explain how merry-go-rounds affect moving objects
questions.explanation: The professor explains the Coriolis effect and how it makes hurricanes rotate.

questions.prompt: According to the professor, what determines the direction in which a sink drains?
options: The hemisphere of the Earth in which the sink is located
The temperature of the water in the sink
The distance of the sink from the equator
The sink's shape and the water's initial motion
questions.explanation: The professor says the direction depends on the sink's shape and how the water was already moving.

questions.prompt: Why does air spin counterclockwise around a hurricane in the Northern Hemisphere?
options: Air flowing inward is deflected to the left.
Air flowing outward is deflected to the right.
Air flowing inward is deflected to the right.
Warm water pushes the air in that direction.
questions.explanation: Inflowing air deflected to the right ends up circling the low-pressure center counterclockwise.

questions.prompt: What can be inferred about why hurricanes rarely form near the equator?
options: Air there is not deflected enough to start rotating.
The ocean there is too cool to supply energy.
The air pressure there is too high to draw air in.
The winds there blow too strongly from the east.
questions.explanation: The Coriolis effect is zero at the equator and weak nearby, so inflowing air does not begin to spin.

intro: Listen to a talk in a paleontology class.
talk: So, how does a living thing become a fossil? Here's the honest answer: almost never. The vast majority of organisms that have ever lived left no trace at all. When an animal dies, scavengers eat it, bacteria decompose it, and weather scatters what's left. For it to become a fossil, it usually has to be buried quickly, by mud on a riverbed, sand in a flood, or ash from a volcano. Burial cuts off oxygen and protects the remains from scavengers. Now, the most common process is called permineralization. Groundwater seeps through the buried bone or wood, and minerals like silica or calcite crystallize in the tiny pores. Over long periods, this makes the remains much harder and heavier, essentially turning them into stone while preserving their shape, sometimes down to the cell structure in petrified wood. So what does this mean for paleontologists? It means the fossil record is biased. Animals with hard parts, like shells, bones, and teeth, are far more likely to be preserved than soft-bodied ones, like jellyfish or worms. And animals that lived in or near water, where sediment builds up, are better represented than ones living on dry hills. It's like trying to understand a city from photos taken only at its harbor. That's why rare sites preserving soft tissues are so valuable.

questions.prompt: What is the talk mainly about?
options: How paleontologists dig up fossils without damage
Why animals with shells evolved before soft animals
How fossils form and why the fossil record is uneven
How petrified wood differs from fossil bone
questions.explanation: The professor explains burial and permineralization and the biases they create in the fossil record.

questions.prompt: Why is quick burial important for fossilization?
options: It supplies minerals that harden the remains at once.
It keeps the remains warm enough to be preserved.
It allows bacteria to break down the soft tissue.
It protects remains from oxygen and scavengers.
questions.explanation: The professor says burial cuts off oxygen and protects remains from scavengers.

questions.prompt: What happens during permineralization?
options: Minerals crystallize in the pores of buried remains.
Bones dissolve and leave an empty mold in the rock.
Soft tissues are replaced by layers of volcanic ash.
Remains are frozen and kept from decaying.
questions.explanation: Groundwater deposits minerals like silica or calcite in the tiny pores of bone or wood.

questions.prompt: Why does the professor mention photos taken only at a harbor?
options: To show that most fossils are found in coastal cities
To illustrate that the fossil record gives an unbalanced picture
To explain how sediment slowly collects at the mouths of large rivers
To suggest that sea animals outnumbered land animals
questions.explanation: Like harbor-only photos, fossils overrepresent animals living near water and with hard parts.

intro: Listen to a talk in a genetics class.
talk: Most of you have heard of CRISPR as a gene-editing tool. But it didn't start in a lab. It started as an immune system in bacteria. Bacteria are constantly attacked by viruses called bacteriophages. Starting in the late nineteen eighties, researchers noticed strange patterns in bacterial DNA: short repeated sequences with unique stretches of DNA between them. For years, nobody knew what they were. Then researchers realized that those in-between stretches matched the DNA of viruses. So here's what's happening. When a bacterium survives a viral attack, it cuts out a small piece of the virus's DNA and stores it in this region, like a mug shot in a police file. Later, the bacterium copies those stored pieces into RNA guides. Each guide teams up with an enzyme that cuts DNA, called Cas nine in the best-known system. If the same virus invades again, the guide recognizes the matching sequence, and the enzyme cuts the virus's DNA, disabling it. Now, why does this matter for gene editing? Because the guide can be reprogrammed. Write a guide to match any sequence, and the enzyme will cut there, in a human cell, a plant, anything. Here's a difference, though. In bacteria, the system's purpose is destruction. In gene editing, the cut is just the first step; the cell's own repair machinery makes the actual change.

options: To describe how viruses copy their DNA inside bacteria
To compare different methods of editing human genes
To explain the natural origin of a gene-editing tool
To explain how bacteria repair their damaged DNA
questions.explanation: The professor explains how CRISPR works as a bacterial immune system and how it was adapted for editing.

questions.prompt: According to the professor, what did researchers discover about the stretches between the repeated sequences?
options: They matched DNA from viruses.
They matched DNA from other bacteria.
They contained the enzyme itself.
They were copied from human cells.

questions.prompt: What happens when a virus invades a bacterium a second time?
options: The bacterium stores a new piece of the viral DNA.
The virus copies the bacterium's RNA guides.
The enzyme repairs the bacterium's damaged DNA.

questions.explanation: The guide recognizes the matching sequence and the enzyme cuts and disables the viral DNA.

options: To explain why bacteria are attacked by viruses so often
To show that it helps the cell recognize a past attacker
To suggest that the stored DNA is harmful to the cell
To describe how scientists traced the virus's origin
questions.explanation: Like a mug shot, the stored sequence is a record used to identify the same virus if it returns.

intro: Listen to a talk in a neuroscience class.
talk: Okay, so here's something that puzzled doctors for centuries. After someone loses an arm, they often continue to feel it: an itch, a cramp, even pain in a hand that's no longer there. These are called phantom limb sensations, and they're reported by a large majority of amputees. So where do they come from? For a long time, the leading explanation was peripheral. The idea was that the cut nerve endings in the stump become irritated and keep sending signals, and the brain interprets those signals as coming from the missing hand. That certainly contributes in some cases. But it can't be the whole story, because phantom sensations can persist even when those nerves are blocked. So researchers turned to the brain itself. In the cortex, there's a region called the somatosensory cortex that works like a map of the body. Interestingly, the face and the hand sit right next to each other on that map. When the hand stops sending input, neighboring areas, like the face region, seem to gradually take over the hand's territory. And some amputees report that touching their cheek produces a sensation in their missing fingers. This is called cortical remapping. But there's a twist. Some recent studies suggest that the hand's map survives remarkably intact, so remapping alone may not explain phantom pain.

questions.prompt: What is the talk mainly about?
options: How doctors treat ongoing pain in the stumps of recent amputees
How the brain's body map develops in children
Explanations for why people feel limbs that are missing
Why the face and the hand share the same nerves
questions.explanation: The professor compares peripheral and brain-based explanations of phantom limb sensations.

questions.prompt: Why does the professor say the peripheral explanation cannot be complete?
options: Cut nerve endings never send any signals to the brain.
Most amputees report no feeling in the missing limb.
The brain cannot tell where nerve signals come from.
Phantom sensations can continue when the nerves are blocked.
questions.explanation: If sensations persist with the stump nerves blocked, irritated nerves can't be the whole cause.

questions.prompt: According to the professor, what happens during cortical remapping?
options: The hand region moves to a completely different part of the cortex.
Nearby areas take over the region that once served the hand.
The face region stops responding to touch on the cheek.
New nerves grow from the stump back into the brain.
questions.explanation: Neighboring regions such as the face area gradually take over the hand's territory.

questions.prompt: What does the professor imply about cortical remapping?
options: It may not fully explain phantom pain.
It occurs only in the brains of children.
It proves the nerves play no role at all.
It happens only when the face is touched.
questions.explanation: Recent studies suggest the hand's map stays largely intact, so remapping alone may not account for phantom pain.

intro: Listen to a talk in a physiology class.
talk: So imagine you fly from a city at sea level straight to a town high in the Andes, around four thousand meters. You'll probably feel short of breath, maybe get a headache. Why? Well, the air up there still contains about twenty-one percent oxygen, the same proportion as at sea level. What's different is the air pressure. It's much lower, so each breath brings in fewer oxygen molecules, roughly forty percent fewer at that height. Now, the body responds in stages. Within minutes, you start breathing faster and deeper, and your heart rate goes up. Over the next few days, your kidneys detect the lower oxygen level in the blood and release a hormone called erythropoietin, or EPO for short. EPO signals the bone marrow to make more red blood cells, the cells that carry oxygen. That takes weeks to really build up, which is why climbers spend time at intermediate camps before going higher. This is called acclimatization, the gradual adjustment of the body to a new environment. It's also why some endurance athletes train at altitude before competing lower down. Now, here's an interesting contrast. Populations that have lived at high altitude for thousands of years, for example in Tibet, don't simply have more red blood cells. Many have fairly normal levels and adapt in other ways, such as breathing more.

questions.prompt: What is the talk mainly about?
options: Why the air holds a smaller share of oxygen up high
How the human body adjusts to high altitude
How athletes train for competitions at sea level
Why people in Tibet have more red blood cells
questions.explanation: The professor describes the stages of acclimatization to the low pressure at high altitude.

questions.prompt: According to the professor, why do people get short of breath at high altitude?
options: Each breath contains fewer oxygen molecules.
The air contains a smaller percentage of oxygen.
The kidneys stop producing an important hormone.
The heart beats more slowly in the thin air.
questions.explanation: The oxygen percentage is the same, but lower pressure means each breath holds fewer oxygen molecules.

questions.prompt: What is the role of EPO?
options: It makes the lungs breathe faster and deeper.
It lets each red blood cell carry more oxygen.
It signals the body to make more red blood cells.
It lowers the heart rate at high altitude.
questions.explanation: The professor says EPO signals the bone marrow to produce more red blood cells.

questions.prompt: Why does the professor mention populations in Tibet?
options: To give an example of people who need more red blood cells
To explain why climbers rest at intermediate camps
To show that EPO is produced only at high altitude
To show that long-term adaptation can work differently
questions.explanation: Many Tibetans adapt by breathing more rather than by having more red blood cells.

intro: Listen to a talk in an astronomy class.
talk: So, how do you find a planet around another star when the planet itself is far too dim to see directly, lost in its star's glare? Astronomers mostly rely on two indirect methods, and they tell us different things. The first is the radial velocity method. A planet doesn't simply orbit its star. Both orbit their shared center of mass, so the star wobbles slightly. When the star moves toward us, its light shifts toward the blue; when it moves away, toward the red. By measuring those tiny shifts, we can detect the planet and estimate its mass. The second is the transit method. If a planet's orbit happens to be lined up with our view, it passes in front of its star and blocks a small fraction of the light. A planet the size of Jupiter dims a sun-like star by about one percent; an Earth-sized planet, by less than a hundredth of that. The amount of dimming tells us the planet's size. Now, here's why combining them is so powerful. Radial velocity gives mass, transits give size, and together they give density. And density tells you what the planet is made of, whether it's rocky like Earth or mostly gas. But there's a limitation. Transits only work for the small fraction of systems we happen to see edge-on.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of the talk?
options: To compare two methods for detecting planets around other stars
To explain why giant planets tend to form close to their stars
To describe how light changes color as it travels through space
To argue that most planets are made mostly of gas
questions.explanation: The professor contrasts the radial velocity and transit methods and what each reveals.

questions.prompt: According to the professor, what causes a star to wobble?
options: The planet passes directly in front of the star's face.
The star's light shifts between blue and red.
The star is pulled by other nearby stars.
The star and planet orbit a shared center of mass.
questions.explanation: Because both bodies orbit their shared center of mass, the star moves slightly.

questions.prompt: What information does the transit method provide about a planet?
options: Its mass
Its size
Its density
Its temperature
questions.explanation: The professor says the amount of dimming tells us the planet's size.

questions.prompt: Why does the professor say that combining the two methods is powerful?
options: Together they detect planets that are not edge-on.
Together they remove the glare of the star.
Together they reveal what a planet is made of.
Together they measure the age of the star.
questions.explanation: Mass from radial velocity and size from transits give density, which indicates composition.

intro: Listen to a talk in a planetary science class.
talk: Today's question: why does Saturn have rings while our Moon is a solid body? The key concept is the Roche limit, named after the nineteenth-century French astronomer who worked it out. Here's the idea. When a moon orbits a planet, the planet's gravity pulls harder on the moon's near side than on its far side. That difference is called a tidal force, and it tries to stretch the moon apart. Meanwhile, the moon's own gravity is trying to hold it together. Now, the closer the moon is to the planet, the stronger that stretching becomes. And there's a distance, the Roche limit, inside which the stretching wins. A moon held together only by its own gravity, a loose pile of rubble or ice, would be torn apart, and the debris would spread out into a ring. And sure enough, Saturn's main rings lie mostly inside its Roche limit, while its large moons orbit outside it. For the same reason, ring material can't clump together to form a new moon there. Our Moon, by contrast, is far outside Earth's Roche limit. But here's a subtlety. Small solid objects, like a spacecraft, can survive inside the limit, because they're held together by the strength of their material, not just by gravity. And how old are Saturn's rings? Some measurements suggest they're surprisingly young, but that's still debated.

questions.prompt: What is the talk mainly about?
options: Why material close to a planet may form rings instead of moons
How tidal forces cause the ocean tides on Earth
Why Saturn's rings are older than its large moons
How astronomers recently measured the exact age of Saturn's rings
questions.explanation: The professor uses the Roche limit to explain why rings form inside a certain distance from a planet.

questions.prompt: According to the professor, what is a tidal force?
options: The pull of a moon's own gravity on its surface
The force that holds ring particles together in clumps
A difference in a planet's pull on two sides of a moon
The force that keeps a moon in a stable orbit
questions.explanation: The professor defines it as the difference between the pull on the near side and on the far side.

questions.prompt: Why can a small, solid object survive inside the Roche limit?
options: Its own gravity is stronger than the planet's.
Its material strength holds it together.
It orbits too fast to feel tidal forces.
It is protected by the surrounding rings.
questions.explanation: Such objects are held together by the strength of their material, not just by gravity.

questions.prompt: What does the professor imply about the age of Saturn's rings?
options: It matches the age of Saturn's large moons.
It explains why the rings lie inside the limit.
It was first calculated by Roche himself.
It has not yet been firmly established.
questions.explanation: She says some measurements suggest the rings are young but the question is still debated.

intro: Listen to a talk in a physics class.
talk: So here's a problem that bothered physicists in the early twentieth century. The Sun shines because, in its core, hydrogen nuclei fuse to form helium. But to fuse, two nuclei have to get extremely close. And since both are positively charged, they repel each other, more and more strongly as they approach. That repulsion acts like a wall, an energy barrier. Now, the core of the Sun is very hot, around fifteen million degrees, so the nuclei are moving fast. But when physicists calculated it, even at that temperature, almost none of them had enough energy to climb over the wall. By classical physics, the Sun shouldn't be shining. So what's going on? The answer is quantum tunneling. In quantum mechanics, a particle is described by a wave that spreads out a bit, and part of that wave extends through the barrier. So there's a small probability that the particle simply appears on the other side, even without enough energy to go over the top. It's as if a ball rolled at a hill too high for it sometimes turned up on the far side. For large everyday objects, that probability is essentially zero. But for a tiny proton, it's small but real. And with an enormous number of collisions every second, that small probability is enough to power the Sun.

questions.prompt: What is the talk mainly about?
options: Why the core of the Sun is so extremely hot
How a quantum effect allows fusion to occur in the Sun
How hydrogen is produced inside young stars
Why protons repel each other so strongly at very short distances
questions.explanation: The professor explains how quantum tunneling lets nuclei fuse despite lacking the energy to overcome repulsion.

questions.prompt: According to the professor, why do hydrogen nuclei repel each other?
options: They move too fast to stay close.
They are surrounded by electron waves.
They both carry a positive charge.
They lose energy as they approach.
questions.explanation: The professor says both nuclei are positively charged, so they repel each other.

questions.prompt: What problem did early calculations reveal?
options: Few nuclei had enough energy to overcome the barrier.
The Sun's core was much cooler than expected.
Hydrogen nuclei did not repel each other strongly.
The Sun contained less hydrogen than predicted.
questions.explanation: Even at fifteen million degrees, almost no nuclei had enough energy to climb over the barrier.

questions.prompt: Why does the professor mention the enormous number of collisions every second?
options: To show why the core of the Sun is so hot
To explain why tunneling never happens to large everyday objects
To show that most nuclei have enough energy
To explain how a rare event can still power the Sun
questions.explanation: A tiny tunneling probability, multiplied by vast numbers of collisions, produces enough fusion.

intro: Listen to a talk in a chemistry class.
talk: Hold up your hands for a second. They're mirror images of each other, but you can't stack one perfectly on top of the other. Chemists call this property chirality, from the Greek word for hand. A chiral molecule is one that can't be superimposed on its mirror image. Usually, it contains a carbon atom bonded to four different groups. The two mirror-image versions are called enantiomers. Now, here's the interesting part. Enantiomers have identical physical properties in most respects: the same melting point, the same boiling point. One measurable difference is that they rotate polarized light in opposite directions. But in the body, they can behave very differently. Why? Because the body's receptors and enzymes are themselves chiral. Think of a glove: a right glove fits only a right hand. So one enantiomer may fit a receptor while its mirror image doesn't. A simple example is carvone. One version smells like spearmint, and the other like caraway seeds. Same atoms, same bonds, different smell. And this has serious consequences for medicine. In some drugs, one enantiomer is effective and the other is useless or even harmful. That's why drug makers now often produce just the useful form. But there's a complication: some molecules convert from one form into the other inside the body, so even a pure dose may not stay pure.

options: Mirror-image molecules and how they can differ
How chemists measure the melting points of molecules
How the sense of smell detects different chemicals
Why carbon forms bonds with four different groups
questions.explanation: The professor explains chirality and why mirror-image molecules can act differently in the body.

questions.prompt: According to the professor, how do enantiomers differ in their physical properties?
options: They have different melting and boiling points.
They rotate polarized light in opposite directions.
They contain different numbers of carbon atoms.
They form different bonds between the same atoms.
questions.explanation: The professor says they share most properties but rotate polarized light in opposite directions.

questions.prompt: Why can enantiomers have different effects in the body?
options: One version breaks down faster in water.
One version contains a harmful atom.
The body's receptors are also chiral.
The body cannot absorb polarized light.
questions.explanation: Because receptors and enzymes are chiral, only one enantiomer may fit, like a glove on a hand.

options: To show how chemists separate the two forms of a drug in the lab
To explain how polarized light is rotated
To give an example of a harmful medicine
To show that mirror-image forms can differ in smell
questions.explanation: Carvone's two forms smell like spearmint and caraway, showing that enantiomers can have different effects.

intro: Listen to a talk in a materials science class.
talk: So, there's a story you may have heard: that old windows in medieval cathedrals are thicker at the bottom because glass is actually a very slow liquid that has flowed downward over the centuries. It's a great story, but it's wrong. Let's see why, and what glass really is. In a crystal, like quartz, atoms are arranged in a regular, repeating pattern. Glass, which is mostly made from the same silica, has no such long-range order. Its atoms are arranged randomly, like a liquid's, but they're locked in place. That's what we call an amorphous solid. How does that happen? When molten silica cools slowly, the atoms have time to find their places in a crystal. But if it cools quickly, it thickens until the atoms are essentially frozen in a disordered arrangement before they can organize. Now, does glass flow at room temperature? Calculations suggest that ordinary glass at room temperature is so viscous that any noticeable sagging would take far longer than the age of the universe. So why are the old windows uneven? Medieval glassmaking simply couldn't produce sheets of uniform thickness, and installers often put the thicker edge at the bottom. And some old panes have the thick edge at the top or the side, which the flowing theory can't explain. So glass is a solid, just not a crystalline one.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of the talk?
options: To describe how medieval cathedrals were constructed
To compare the strength of glass and quartz crystals
To explain how glassmaking techniques have improved
To correct a myth by explaining the structure of glass
questions.explanation: The professor explains that glass is an amorphous solid and refutes the flowing-window story.

questions.prompt: According to the professor, how does glass differ from quartz?
options: It is made from a different main ingredient.
Its atoms move freely at room temperature.
Its atoms lack a regular, repeating pattern.
It forms only when silica cools slowly.
questions.explanation: Glass has no long-range order; its atoms are arranged randomly but locked in place.

options: Its atoms arrange themselves into a regular pattern.
Its atoms become fixed before they can form a crystal.
It stays liquid until it reaches room temperature.
It flows downward and becomes thicker at the bottom.
questions.explanation: Rapid cooling freezes the atoms in a disordered arrangement before they can organize.

options: To provide evidence against the flowing-glass explanation
To show that medieval glass slowly flowed in several different directions
To explain why installers preferred uneven glass
To show that modern glass is more uniform than old glass
questions.explanation: Glass flowing downward could not produce a thick edge at the top or side.

intro: Listen to a talk in a climatology class.
talk: Today we're looking at why the Arctic is warming much faster than the planet as a whole, by some estimates nearly four times faster. Scientists call this Arctic amplification. So what drives it? The best-known factor is the ice-albedo feedback. Albedo is the fraction of sunlight a surface reflects. Snow and sea ice have a high albedo, reflecting most sunlight. Dark open ocean has a low albedo, absorbing most of it. Think of wearing a white shirt versus a black shirt on a sunny day. Now, here's the feedback. As temperatures rise, sea ice melts, exposing dark water. The water absorbs more sunlight and warms, which melts more ice, and so on. It's a loop that reinforces itself. But here's where it gets interesting. Climate models show amplification still happens even when the ice-albedo feedback is switched off. So it can't be the only factor. Another major factor involves how the atmosphere is structured. In the Arctic, especially in winter, the air near the ground is often colder than the air above it. Because of that, warming stays trapped near the surface instead of being mixed upward. And cold surfaces shed extra heat to space less efficiently, so the poles must warm more to get rid of it. So researchers now see amplification as several feedbacks working together, and they still debate which matters most.

options: How scientists measure the albedo of sea ice
Why the Arctic is colder in winter than summer
How climate models predict future snowfall
Why the Arctic is warming unusually fast
questions.explanation: The professor discusses several feedbacks that cause Arctic amplification.

options: Darker water is exposed and absorbs more sunlight.
More sunlight is reflected back into space.
Cold air from above mixes down to the surface.
The albedo of the surrounding ocean increases.
questions.explanation: Melting exposes dark, low-albedo water that absorbs more sunlight and warms further.

options: The Arctic stopped warming altogether.
The Arctic warmed at the global average rate.
The Arctic still warmed faster than other regions.
The Arctic cooled because of increased snow.
questions.explanation: The professor says amplification still happens without that feedback, so other factors must contribute.

options: To explain why warm air stays trapped close to the Arctic surface
To illustrate the difference between high and low albedo
To show how sea ice forms during the winter months
To compare the temperatures of land and ocean
questions.explanation: White reflects sunlight like snow and ice, while black absorbs it like open water.

intro: Listen to a talk in a mathematics history class.
talk: For more than two thousand years, one statement in geometry bothered mathematicians more than any other. Around three hundred BCE, Euclid built his geometry on five basic assumptions, or postulates. The first four are simple, like, a straight line can be drawn between any two points. But the fifth, the parallel postulate, is long and awkward. In a common modern form, it says that through a point not on a given line, exactly one line can be drawn parallel to it. Many mathematicians felt it should be provable from the other four. So, for centuries, they tried. Some attempted proof by contradiction: assume the postulate is false, and show that this leads to an absurdity. And here's the irony. They derived strange results, like triangles whose angles add up to less than one hundred eighty degrees, but they never found a true contradiction. In the early eighteen hundreds, the Russian Nikolai Lobachevsky and the Hungarian János Bolyai, working independently, took the bold step of accepting those strange results as a consistent geometry in its own right. Now, this means the parallel postulate can't be proven from the others. There are other perfectly valid geometries. On a sphere, for instance, a triangle's angles add up to more than one hundred eighty degrees. Later, these geometries proved useful for describing space in physics.

questions.prompt: What is the talk mainly about?
options: Why Euclid's first four postulates were later rejected
How the angles of a triangle are measured on a sphere
How attempts to prove a postulate led to new geometries
Why Russian and Hungarian mathematicians worked together
questions.explanation: The professor explains how failed proofs of the parallel postulate led to non-Euclidean geometry.

questions.prompt: Why did many mathematicians try to prove the parallel postulate?
options: They thought it should follow from the other four.
They believed it contradicted the other four.
They wanted to simplify Euclid's first postulate.
They needed it to measure triangles on a sphere.
questions.explanation: The professor says they felt it wasn't a basic assumption and should be provable from the others.

questions.prompt: According to the professor, what did Lobachevsky and Bolyai do?
options: They finally proved the parallel postulate.
They accepted the strange results as a valid geometry.
They worked together to find a contradiction.
They showed that Euclid's geometry was internally inconsistent.
questions.explanation: Working independently, they treated the strange results as a consistent geometry in its own right.

questions.prompt: What is ironic about the attempts at proof by contradiction?
options: They proved that the fifth postulate was true.
They showed that triangles cannot exist on a sphere.
They found a contradiction in the first four postulates.
They produced a new geometry instead of a proof.
questions.explanation: Instead of reaching a contradiction, the strange results became the basis of a new, valid geometry.
